rows.practice: analyses political ideas, actors, institutions and behaviour with a range of concepts, theories and methods, gathering and interpreting qualitative or quantitative political data
rows.knowledge: power as a contested concept, the main approaches to studying politics and international relations and how national and international political systems are structured and operate
rows.identity: a student of politics who conducts research ethically, reflects critically on their own learning and takes part in multicultural settings at home and abroad

rows.practice: frames research questions and hypotheses, reviews the literature critically and plans and runs a self-directed project that interprets evidence soundly and joins the field's debates
rows.knowledge: the normative and explanatory roots of political ideas, the historical, social, economic and cultural contexts of political action and rival accounts of political change
rows.identity: a critical analyst of politics who weighs the ethical consequences of research, judges competing readings of events and questions the vocabulary of political debate

digest.definition: The field studies power, governance, participation, decision-making, conflict and cooperation at every scale, from local to global
distinctiveFeatures: The field studies power, governance, participation, decision-making, conflict and cooperation at every scale, from local to global

Politics asks who gets what, when, how, why and where, around questions of power, justice, legitimacy, sovereignty and security; international relations adds a world split into many polities, states and the actors above, below and beyond them

Its ways of knowing combine description, general explanation, normative theory and political philosophy, positive political theory and approaches that reject universal theories, such as historical and postmodern analysis
It uses a wide range of quantitative and qualitative methods and draws on cognate subjects
Its boundaries and names are contested and shifting, and it treats its own history (imperial, colonial, patriarchal and other) as an object of critical study
It prepares graduates for careers, active citizenship and leading change, in policy, enterprise, public institutions and beyond

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: the subject's own matter is power, privilege and exclusion; students examine how the discipline was shaped by and helped shape colonialism, patriarchy and racism and read marginalised scholars; course teams build inclusive communities and close gaps in access, attainment and awarding (D1, 1.11 to 1.13)
courses designed to be accessible to all, attainment and experience gaps reduced, reasonable adjustments in place (D1, 1.13, 1.14)

headed Sustainability in the text: integral to how the subject studies an interconnected world, quoting the ESD guidance, to run through the whole course and framed by the SDGs; climate breakdown, inequality, misinformation; sustainability and environmental politics as a subfield (D1, 1.15 to 1.18, 3.2)

a key component of the degree: an inquisitive, adaptable mindset and competencies such as negotiation, influence and evidence-based problem solving, built through placements, simulations and authentic assessment such as policy briefs (D1, 1.19 to 1.22, 3.14)

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Politics and International Relations degree
Context and purposes of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.appliesTo: students on taught postgraduate courses in the subject
statements.about: a higher level of learning on taught master's courses
statements.paraphrase: The statement describes the discipline and guides the standards expected of honours graduates, chiefly for single honours and for joint honours where the subject is at least half the curriculum; taught postgraduate degrees at FHEQ level 7 and FQHEIS level 11 rest on the same principles but require students to show a higher level of learning, usually with more specialist content.

forPractitioner.text: Taught master's courses in the subject share the honours principles, but their students must demonstrate a higher level of learning, usually with deeper specialist content, at FHEQ level 7 or FQHEIS level 11.

forBeneficiary.text: If you go on to a taught master's in politics or international relations, you must show a higher level of learning than at honours, usually with more specialised content.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.about: education for sustainable development across the whole course
statements.paraphrase: Education for sustainable development lets the discipline question its established approaches and should run through degree courses rather than sit only in specialist modules; a review of curriculum and teaching against the ESD guidance, and the UN SDGs as a frame, can help embed it.

forPractitioner.text: Embed education for sustainable development across the whole course, not only in specialist options; reviewing curriculum and teaching against the ESD guidance, and using the SDGs as a frame, can show where it should sit.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to embed sustainability; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.about: course design: outcomes, formats and core content
statements.paraphrase: Courses offer structured pathways that build what an honours degree needs and that students can use for good in their own lives and communities; each course design will set out its learning outcomes and its forms of learning, teaching and assessment, with the content core to those outcomes.

forPractitioner.text: Each course's design will state its learning outcomes and its learning, teaching and assessment formats, naming the content that is core to meeting those outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.about: regular review of curriculum and learning resources
statements.paraphrase: Because politics and the discipline both keep changing, curriculum and learning resources must be reviewed and updated regularly, with educators working with students as partners and co-producers and drawing on pedagogic research.

forPractitioner.text: Review and update the curriculum and learning resources regularly as politics and the discipline change, involving students as partners and co-producers and drawing on pedagogic research in the subject and in higher education.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to keep its curriculum current

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.about: progression through the levels towards the threshold
statements.paraphrase: Over an honours degree (FHEQ level 6; FQHEIS level 10) students will progress level by level under each provider's rules, building towards the threshold subject-specific and generic skills, usually by gaining credit for all learning and assessment including practical parts; a second-class degree or above would normally equip a graduate for postgraduate study, though entry is for each provider to decide.

forPractitioner.text: Students will move through the levels of study by the provider's rules, each level building towards the threshold skills in 4.3 to 4.5, usually by gaining credit for all learning and assessment; a second-class result or better is expected to prepare a graduate for postgraduate study, subject to each provider's entry rules.

forBeneficiary.text: You will move up through the levels of your degree under your university's rules, each year building towards the minimum skills you need by graduation; with a second-class degree or better you would usually be ready for postgraduate study, though each course sets its own entry rules.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.appliesTo: students on joint, combined or major-minor routes
statements.paraphrase: Students on combined, joint or major-minor routes will meet the core outcomes for the subject and add others from their other subjects, with further chances to work across disciplines.

forPractitioner.text: On joint, combined or major-minor routes, students will still achieve the subject's core outcomes and will add outcomes from their other subjects, exploring where the disciplines meet.

forBeneficiary.text: If politics or international relations is one part of a joint or combined degree, you will still meet its core outcomes and gain others from your other subject, with chances to work across both.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.about: the student voice in course monitoring and review
statements.paraphrase: Degree-awarding bodies and their partners gather and analyse information and review courses periodically; the student voice will be part of this, alongside external reference points such as this statement.

forPractitioner.text: Course monitoring and periodic review will take account of the student voice, alongside data and external reference points such as this statement, to keep provision in line with sector norms.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider's review process

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Politics and International Relations degree

statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance: providers will use external reviewers in periodic review to gain an outside view of proposed changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Periodic review will draw on external reviewers to check proposed changes, confirm threshold standards are achieved and judge whether content is right for the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider

statements.about: conceptual and empirical study across several subfields
statements.paraphrase: Students will study the discipline's conceptual and empirical sides and, though scope varies by course, will typically develop and show knowledge and understanding of several of seventeen listed subfields, from area studies to environmental politics.

forPractitioner.text: Every course will cover both conceptual and empirical aspects; students will typically build and demonstrate knowledge of a number of the listed subfields, not all of them, with the mix left to the course.

forBeneficiary.text: You will study both the ideas and the real-world evidence of politics, and you will usually come to know several of its main subfields well, such as comparative politics, political theory or international security.

statements.about: a wide learning environment and many kinds of source
statements.paraphrase: Students should have access to a broad learning environment, from published literature, software and computing to primary sources, archives and data, and should meet and engage with a wide range of sources, with support to judge their value and significance in context.

forPractitioner.text: Give students access to a wide learning environment (literature, digital tools and software, primary sources, archives, statistical data and more), expose them to a broad range of sources and support them to evaluate those sources critically in context.

forBeneficiary.text: You should have access to a wide range of sources, from books and articles to archives, data and media, and get help to judge how useful and reliable each is in different settings.

statements.paraphrase: Assessment and feedback are central to course design; assessments should aim to help students reflect critically on their learning and abilities, let them show their understanding and that they have met learning outcomes and can build skills for personal development, employability and citizenship.

forPractitioner.text: Design assessment so that it aims to enable students to reflect critically on their learning and abilities, while letting them show they have met the course outcomes and building skills for employability and citizenship.

statements.about: diverse assessment so every student can show their abilities

forPractitioner.text: Use a varied range of assessment so that every student, whatever their educational background, has chances to show what they have learned and can do.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course

statements.about: constructive feedback and plural approaches to contested questions
statements.paraphrase: Feedback helps students judge their progress and how to improve; students should receive constructive feedback throughout, with attention to self-reflection and self-criticism, and because core concepts are contested, the range of legitimate approaches to a question should be acknowledged and discussed.

forPractitioner.text: Give constructive feedback throughout the course that builds students' self-reflection and self-criticality, and acknowledge and discuss the range of legitimate approaches to a question, since the subject's core concepts are contested.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to give feedback; the student-facing side is 4.5.b6

statements.paraphrase: Feedback should be both formative and summative and should focus on helping students see how to improve their work, for the task and for their wider skills; formative assessment and feedback work best early, during and after assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Provide formative as well as summative feedback, focused on feedforward: how students can improve, both on the task in hand and in their wider skills.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to give feedback

statements.about: performance above threshold and the classification descriptions
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do much better than the threshold; each provider sets its own way of evidencing this and should refer to Annex D, which describes the four honours classes (1st, 2.1, 2.2 and 3rd) for degrees at FHEQ level 6 and FQHEIS level 10.

forPractitioner.text: Expect most students to exceed the threshold; judge by how much using your own method, referring to Annex D's descriptions of the four classes of honours degree.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in classifying degrees

statements.about: critical familiarity with the concept of power
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show familiarity with power as a concept and engage with it critically, across the four aspects listed beneath this item.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should know the concept of power well and handle it critically, covering four aspects: contested knowledge; approaches to the discipline; its key concepts, theories and methods; and their strengths and weaknesses (4.3.b2 to b5).

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should know your way around the idea of power and be able to question how it is used and understood.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b1: should be able to show that what counts as knowledge and understanding in the subject is open to dispute.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should recognise that knowledge and understanding in the discipline are contested, and treat power as part of that contest.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should understand that what counts as knowledge in politics is itself argued over, and that power shapes those arguments.

statements.about: approaches to studying politics or international relations
statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b1: should know the main approaches to studying politics or international relations.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should know the principal approaches by which politics or international relations is studied, and how each treats power.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should know the main ways scholars go about studying politics or international relations.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b1: should know a range of the central concepts, theories and methods used in the discipline.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should command a range of the discipline's central concepts, theories and methods, in politics or in international relations.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should know a good range of the main ideas, theories and research methods used in your subject.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b1: should be able to weigh what the approaches to the discipline do well and where they fall short.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should judge the strengths and limitations of the discipline's approaches, not only describe them.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to say what each approach to the subject does well and where it falls short.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to engage critically with politics and international relations as fields, across the five aspects listed beneath this item.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should engage critically with the discipline, including its normative and positive foundations, its vocabulary, political and international systems, the contexts of political behaviour and the causes of political change (4.3.b7 to b11).

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to think critically about politics and international relations as subjects, not only learn their content.

statements.about: normative and positive foundations of political ideas
statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b6: should be able to engage critically with both the value-based and the explanatory roots of political ideas.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should engage critically with political ideas from both their normative (what ought to be) and positive (what is, and why) foundations.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to question political ideas both as claims about what ought to be and as explanations of what happens.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b6: should be able to use and question the language in which political debate is conducted.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should handle the vocabulary of political debate critically, using its terms accurately and noticing how they are contested.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to use the language of political argument accurately and notice when its terms are being stretched or contested.

statements.about: how political and international systems are built and work
statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b6: should be able to engage critically with how different political and international systems are built and how they work.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should analyse critically how political and international systems differ in structure and in operation.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to explain and question how different political and international systems are set up and how they work in practice.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b6: should be able to engage critically with the social, economic, historical and cultural settings in which people act politically.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should place political behaviour in its wider settings (social, economic, historical, cultural) and reason critically about how these shape it.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to explain how society, the economy, history and culture shape the way people behave politically.

statements.paraphrase: As part of 4.3.b6: should be able to engage critically with explanations of why political change happens.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should assess critically the factors offered to explain political change.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to weigh up different explanations of why politics changes.

statements.about: applying concepts, theories and methods in political analysis
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to use a variety of concepts, theories and methods to analyse political ideas, actors, institutions and behaviour.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should put concepts, theories and methods to work in analysing political ideas, actors, institutions and behaviour, choosing among them.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to choose and use concepts, theories and methods to analyse political ideas, the people and bodies involved and how they behave.

statements.about: judging interpretations of political issues and events
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to scrutinise and judge competing readings of political issues and events.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should examine and evaluate rival interpretations of political issues and events and reach a reasoned view.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to look at different readings of a political issue or event and judge which holds up best.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to pick a topic suitable for research.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should be able to settle on a research topic that is workable and worth pursuing.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to choose a topic that works for a piece of research.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to form research questions and hypotheses and judge their quality.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should develop research questions and hypotheses and evaluate whether they are clear, answerable and worth testing.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to write research questions and hypotheses and judge whether they are good ones.

statements.about: the ethics of research and enquiry
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to judge and analyse the ethical consequences of research and enquiry.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should weigh and analyse the ethical implications of their own research and enquiry, beyond completing an ethics form.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to think through the ethical questions your research raises and deal with them.

statements.about: methods of data collection and analysis
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to find, understand and use suitable methods for gathering and analysing qualitative or quantitative data, or both.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should identify, interpret and apply methods of data collection and analysis fitted to the question, qualitative, quantitative or both.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to choose, understand and use the right methods to collect and analyse data, whether numbers, words or both.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to search systematically for the literature most relevant to a research topic, from books and reviews to papers and articles, and pick it out.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should search the literature methodically and identify the most relevant books, reviews, papers and articles for a topic.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to search methodically for the most useful books, reviews and articles on your topic.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to review a topic's literature and assess it critically so as to take part in the field's debates, concepts and empirical findings.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should read a topic's literature critically and use it to take part in the field's competing debates, concepts and empirical findings.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to read critically what has been written on a topic and use it to join the debates in your field.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to plan, run and present a self-directed project that shows time management, problem solving, independence and sound interpretation and evaluation of evidence.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should plan, carry out and present a substantial piece of work of their own, showing that they manage time, solve problems, work on their own and weigh the quality of evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to plan, carry out and present a project of your own, managing your time, solving problems as they come and judging how good your evidence is.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to show awareness of relevant theoretical and empirical perspectives and be able to recognise and use them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should know which theoretical and empirical perspectives bear on a question and be able to pick them out and put them to use.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should know which theories and bodies of evidence matter for a question and be able to use them.

statements.about: communicating in varied formats to varied audiences
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to communicate well in a range of formats and to different audiences.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should communicate effectively in varied formats and adapt to different audiences.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to get your point across well in different formats and to different kinds of audience.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to finish tasks efficiently.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should complete tasks efficiently, meeting deadlines without loss of quality.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to get tasks done efficiently.

statements.about: working independently and in a team
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to work both alone and as a member of a team.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should work effectively on their own and within a team.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to work well on your own and with others in a team.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to judge how accurate and reliable sources are and use that judgement to discuss and apply evidence suitably.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should evaluate sources for accuracy and reliability and let that evaluation govern how they discuss and use evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to check how accurate and reliable a source is and use that check when you discuss and use evidence.

statements.paraphrase: Should be able to create and produce information and media in new and inventive ways.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should create and produce information and media innovatively, in forms suited to the purpose.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to make information and media of your own in fresh, inventive ways.

statements.about: using feedback to improve own work
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to take in and reflect on feedback so as to analyse their own work critically and improve it.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should recognise and reflect on feedback and use it to analyse critically and improve their own work.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to take feedback on board, think about it and use it to judge and improve your own work.

statements.about: working with numerical, textual and other data
statements.paraphrase: Should be able to interpret, analyse, apply and present data, whether numerical, textual or other.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should interpret, analyse, apply and present data of several kinds: numerical, textual and others.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should be able to make sense of, analyse, use and present data, whether numbers, texts or other kinds.
